I could be wrong, but I think the way the spec is currently defined, lazy-loaded images do not block the load event, just as images added to the document _after_ the load event has been fired don't block the (already-fired) load event.

I think the biggest thing to do here is as previously discussed, make this language more explicit. Does that make sense?

body:
> https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4-d_SoCHeWE

tl;dw:

1. [2:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4-d_SoCHeWE&feature=youtu.be&t=134) `width` and `height` attributes solved jankiness from images on the web.
2. [3:50](https://youtu.be/4-d_SoCHeWE?t=222) developers wanted responsive images, achieved by applying CSS `width: 100%`, `height: auto`;  _re-introducing jank_.
3. [4:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4-d_SoCHeWE&feature=youtu.be&t=289) UAs add new styles to fix the re-introduced jank:
    > The UA-stylesheets of all browsers will add this code:
    > 
    > ```CSS
    > img, video {
    >     aspect-ratio: attr(width) / attr(height);
    > } 
    >```

    ‐ _https://github.com/WICG/intrinsicsize-attribute/issues/16_

With that, _my conclusion_ is that it really only matters that the `width` and `height` attributes are specified properly, if developers want to set arbitrary pixels in CSS for images, then _I think_ the importance is that they try to maintain the aspect-ratio (`width: {x}`, `height: auto`).

<!--
While the convention for responsive images is to set `height: auto; width: 100%` (recommended in the video in conjunction to `height` and `width` attributes), an author might as well set an arbitrary width/height in pixels using CSS, in that case I _think_ the importance is to always maintain aspect-ratio (only changing `width`, keep `height` as `auto`). So to my understanding, other than maintaining aspect-ratio, all that is really needed is `width` and `height` attributes.
-->
